cells.tense: Right now the thing you kept doing quietly is showing on you, and you can feel the difference.
cells.ask: Teach one piece of what you've refined to somebody earlier on than you, in one sitting, and let them try it while you watch.
cells.core:
People can see the light on you, and it isn't performance. You stayed at the bench past the point where it was interesting, and the repetition stopped being effort and became something you can rely on without checking. You followed what you actually wanted instead of what looked good to want, which is why the thing holds up when someone leans on it.

What that gives you is sight. You can look at someone else's work and see the pattern under it, the one they're too close to see, and you can hand that over without dressing it up. Say it plainly, let them keep it or drop it. Nothing about the shine asks you to protect it now. It came from hours nobody watched, and it stands there whether or not anyone is watching.
cells.sheetLine: What you built away from eyes now shows, and it holds.
cells.verb: following the pull toward what you actually want
cells.place: the bench where repetition turns intention into skill

cells.tense: You're aiming every session at a version of this that hasn't shown up, and the aiming keeps you out of today.
cells.ask: Before today's practice, write down what the next right step actually is, then do only that step and stop when it's done.
cells.core:
There's a later version of this — where the skill is finished, where it lands — and most of your hours are spent living there. So each session gets pointed at the arrival, and the light you're putting out runs ahead of anything built. It comes across as brightness with nothing under it yet, and people step back from that without being able to say why.

The bench is still right here, and today's plain hour is what keeps getting skipped. What's underneath the projection isn't certainty, it's the wish for it. What you attend to before you start is the whole game: choose the smallest real thing to know, then do it and stop. The shine that holds comes from finished work, not from announced work.

cells.tense: The bench is still here, and the hours you give it have thinned out to almost nothing.
cells.ask: Do ten unhurried minutes of the practice today and tell no one it happened, then let that be enough.
cells.core:
The bench stands where it stands, and you're not at it much. The pull that used to bring you back has gone quiet, and sitting down has stopped being the shape of the day. That doesn't read as laziness from the inside. It reads as something you used to turn toward and now don't.

Pushing effort into a tired place just confirms the tiredness. Force is the wrong tool; the practice wants tending, not demanding. Ten quiet minutes with nothing riding on them, nobody told, no result checked, keeps the thing alive at low fuel. You're not being asked to want it back. You're being asked to keep the bench warm so that when the pull turns toward it again, the way is familiar.
cells.sheetLine: The bench is still yours. The pull toward it has gone quiet.

cells.tense: You're already the one people bring this to, and you keep talking about it as if it were ahead of you.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person what you can do now, in plain words, without listing what you still can't.
cells.core:
Someone in the room asks about the very thing you spent your repetitions on, and you answer easily, and then you file the exchange under something smaller — under being helpful, or just having opinions. The shine is running. The saying-so isn't. That's the whole of it: not a lack, a naming that hasn't happened.

There's another face of the same thing, and you'll know if it's yours — the light gone out while you assume it's still lit, because checking stopped rather than because anything changed. Either way the move is one sentence, said to one person, about what you can actually do, standing as true whether or not the work is finished. It isn't finished. That was not the condition for the light.

attempts.check: I cannot see whether a body of work actually reached completion or actually withered — I only have the seat and the status, so each core has to describe the mechanism in a moment the person could recognise and leave the verdict to them. A reader might say 'you don't know what my practice has been', which is fair; the ask is built to survive that, since it is an act they choose, not a fix I'm promising. The sentence that serves me more than them would be any line telling them their practice has flowered or that their hope was defeated — both are verdicts I haven't earned, so neither appears. I have also kept the draw and the seat from trading places: the pull toward the light is what you steer by, and the seat is the bench you refine at, in every status.
